newsitem.title: USA: Senate committee to act on liability bill.
newsitem.headline: Senate committee to act on liability bill.

text.p: The Senate Commerce Committee has scheduled a meeting next Thursday to act on a new version of a bill limiting damages in product liability cases, a committee aide said Friday.

The bill was introduced Thursday night by Sen. Slade Gorton, a Washington state Republican. It is co-sponsored by Senate Majority Leader Trent Lott, a Mississippi Republican, and Arizona Republican John McCain, chairman of the Commerce Committee.

It would limit punitive damages in product liability cases to two times economic damage, or $250,000, whichever is greater. It sets a limit of two years after the harm caused by the product for filing suits and allows defendants to cite the use of alcohol or drugs by the plaintiffs as a defence.
Gorton said the bill was a modification of one vetoed by President Clinton last year after it passed Congress.

"I wanted to craft another bill that would obtain bi-partisan support in the Senate, address the president's legitimate concerns with the conference report and accomplish meaningful reform," he said in a statement. "I introduce this measure to get the process started."
West Virginia Democrat Jay Rockefeller, a key co-sponsor of last year's bill, did not endorse Gorton's measure.
Supporters of product liability reform say limits are needed to curb excessive damage awards and discourage frivolous lawsuits.

Clinton vetoed last year's bill because he said it went too far in limiting the rights of injury victims to sue, but supporters of the bill said he was influenced by trial lawyers who contributed heavily to his campaign. Trial lawyers get fees based on the damages awarded in liability cases.
Meanwhile, the full Senate is scheduled to debate and vote on a bill to provide protection from liability suits for volunteers of nonprofit organisations.
